summary: Chinese silvergrass is a large, clump-forming grass that is widely sold as an ornamental. On New York's invasive species list it is a regulated species: it is legal to buy, sell and grow, but it is illegal to release it into the wild. Some escaped populations stay as one or a few clumps, while others form large stands that spread quickly; on Long Island, stands covering many acres have been seen at Heckscher State Park and Seatuck National Wildlife Refuge. Its dead leaves and stems burn very hot and fast, so it may make fires more frequent and intense.
history: Chinese silvergrass is native to eastern Asia. It has spread through sales of many garden varieties, and has also been introduced for bioenergy. Its seeds can travel on clothing and in yard waste.
seasons: Its seeds have long hairs and are carried by the wind. Flowering times vary a lot between varieties, and some bloom so late that they cannot set seed before frost.

handling.text: Small patches can be pulled by hand, but this works less well for large stands. Cutting it close to the ground repeatedly through the growing season for two years kills most plants, though more follow-up may be needed because seeds stay in the soil. Plants in wetlands are harder to remove.

report:
New York's official database for invasive species sightings is iMapInvasives, run by the New York Natural Heritage Program (a partnership between SUNY ESF and the NYS Department of Environmental Conservation). You can make a free account and report directly to the online database, which is the preferred method, or use the iMapInvasives mobile app for iPhone and Android, which can upload your records once you have a connection again. If you don't want an account, the site has a public report form; those reports are reviewed by Natural Heritage Program staff each week before being added.

In New York City parks, report what you find instead of removing it yourself. NYC Parks rules forbid cutting, killing or removing any plants, flowers, shrubs or other vegetation without permission from the Parks Commissioner, and forbid chasing, harassing, harming or removing any animal, nest, or the eggs of any amphibian, reptile or bird (56 RCNY §1-04).
